prompt: Which statement best distinguishes income from wealth?

options.label: A
options.text: Income and wealth are both annual flows.

options.label: B
options.text: Income includes wages; wealth includes all other annual receipts.

options.label: C
options.text: Income is a flow; wealth is a stock.

options.label: D
options.text: Income is a stock; wealth is an annual flow.

explanation: Income is measured per period, such as wages per week or interest per year. Wealth is the accumulated value of assets, such as property, savings and shares, measured at a particular point in time.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which is an example of wealth rather than income?

options.label: A
options.text: The salary earned each month from the individual’s current employment during the year

options.label: B
options.text: The value of a house owned by an individual

options.label: C
options.text: The rent received from a tenant during the year

options.label: D
options.text: The annual interest received on savings

explanation: A house is an asset and forms part of a person’s stock of wealth. Salary, interest and rent received are flows of income over a period.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which is an example of income rather than wealth?

options.label: A
options.text: The balance in a savings account

options.label: B
options.text: The market value of the individual’s shareholdings on a specified date, before any dividend payment

options.label: C
options.text: The value of land owned

options.label: D
options.text: Dividends received from shares during the year

explanation: Dividends are a flow received from ownership of shares. The shares themselves, savings balances and land are assets and therefore part of wealth.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A person has $40 000 in a bank account and receives $1200 interest during the year. How should these be classified?

options.label: A
options.text: $40 000 is wealth; $1200 is income.

options.label: B
options.text: The $40 000 account balance and the $1200 received during the year are both flows of income.

options.label: C
options.text: $40 000 is income; $1200 is wealth.

options.label: D
options.text: $40 000 and $1200 are both wealth.

explanation: The bank balance is a stock of financial assets at a point in time. Interest is a flow earned from that asset during the year.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why can a person with substantial wealth have a relatively low current income?

options.label: A
options.text: Assets may be valuable without generating much current income.

options.label: B
options.text: Wealth must be smaller than the individual's annual income.

options.label: C
options.text: Income and wealth must always rise in the same proportions.

options.label: D
options.text: Asset values must automatically be paid out as annual wages.

explanation: Wealth measures the value of assets, not the size of current receipts. A valuable house, for example, may form a large part of wealth without generating a cash income for its owner.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO2 Analysis

prompt: How can wealth generate income?

options.label: A
options.text: Assets generate receipts such as rent, interest and dividends.

options.label: B
options.text: Assets generate receipts only when the government taxes their value.

options.label: C
options.text: Assets must disappear whenever their owners receive an income payment.

options.label: D
options.text: Assets are created automatically whenever individuals receive wage payments.

explanation: Ownership of assets can create income streams. Property may earn rent, bank deposits may earn interest and shares may pay dividends.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which measurement is a stock concept?

options.label: A
options.text: The total pension payments received by the household during December and accumulated across the rest of the current year.

options.label: B
options.text: The wages earned by a household during December.

options.label: C
options.text: The interest received by a household during December.

options.label: D
options.text: The assets owned by a household on 31 December.

explanation: A stock is measured at a particular date. Wages, interest and pensions are flows measured over a period.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A government pays an unemployment benefit each week. For the recipient, the payment is best described as

options.label: A
options.text: A stock of wealth measured at one date.

options.label: B
options.text: A physical asset owned at one date.

options.label: C
options.text: A flow of income received over time.

options.label: D
options.text: A tax on capital held over time.

explanation: A transfer payment is received during a period and therefore contributes to the recipient’s income flow, even though it is not a reward for providing a factor service.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What does a Gini coefficient measure?

options.label: A
options.text: The share of the labour force currently without employment.

options.label: B
options.text: The degree of inequality in an income or wealth distribution.

options.label: C
options.text: The average real income received by each person in an economy.

options.label: D
options.text: The growth rate of real output produced in an economy.

explanation: The Gini coefficient is a measure of how unequally income or wealth is distributed. It does not by itself measure average income, growth or unemployment.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.2 measuring income and wealth inequality: Gini coefficient (calculation not required) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which Gini coefficient indicates the most equal distribution?
explanation: A lower Gini coefficient indicates a more equal distribution. A value closer to zero therefore represents less inequality.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.2 measuring income and wealth inequality: Gini coefficient (calculation not required) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What does a Gini coefficient of 0 represent in theory?

options.label: A
options.text: Complete inequality in the measured distribution.

options.label: B
options.text: Complete equality in the measured distribution.

options.label: C
options.text: Zero income earned throughout the economy.

options.label: D
options.text: Zero wealth owned throughout the economy.

explanation: At the theoretical lower bound of zero, the relevant income or wealth is distributed equally. The coefficient describes distribution, not the total amount available.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.2 measuring income and wealth inequality: Gini coefficient (calculation not required) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A country’s Gini coefficient falls from 0.46 to 0.39. What can be concluded?

options.label: A
options.text: The distribution has become more equal.

options.label: B
options.text: Average income has fallen.

options.label: C
options.text: The distribution has become more unequal.

options.label: D
options.text: Every household must have become richer because a reduction in measured inequality necessarily raises all individual incomes.

explanation: A fall in the Gini coefficient indicates a reduction in inequality. It does not reveal whether average income rose or fell or whether every household gained.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.2 measuring income and wealth inequality: Gini coefficient (calculation not required) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Country X has a Gini coefficient of 0.31 and country Y has a coefficient of 0.48. What can be concluded?

options.label: A
options.text: X necessarily has higher average income.

options.label: B
options.text: X has the more equal measured distribution.

options.label: C
options.text: Y necessarily has a larger total population.

options.label: D
options.text: Y has the more equal measured distribution.

explanation: The Gini coefficient ranks the degree of inequality. It gives no direct information about the average level of income, the income of particular people or population size.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.2 measuring income and wealth inequality: Gini coefficient (calculation not required) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Two economies have the same Gini coefficient. Which statement must be correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Their average incomes are identical.

options.label: B
options.text: Every household in both economies receives exactly the same income because equal coefficients imply complete equality.

options.label: C
options.text: Their measured inequality is equal despite possibly different incomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Their total asset values are identical.

explanation: Identical Gini coefficients indicate the same measured degree of inequality, not identical income levels or identical distributions in every detail.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.2 measuring income and wealth inequality: Gini coefficient (calculation not required) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which change is most likely to increase income inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: Narrowing wage differences through greater access to qualifications.

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing disposable-income differences through a more progressive income-tax schedule while other income sources remain unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: Narrowing income differences through reduced long-term unemployment.

options.label: D
options.text: Widening wage differences between high-skilled and low-skilled workers.

explanation: A larger wage differential directly widens earned-income differences. Better qualifications, lower unemployment and more progressive taxation would normally work in the opposite direction.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why can unemployment increase income inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployment makes income taxation progressively more equal.

options.label: B
options.text: Unemployment raises every employed worker's earnings equally.

options.label: C
options.text: Unemployment turns earned income into accumulated wealth.

options.label: D
options.text: Unemployment reduces affected households' earned income sharply.

explanation: Those without work lose wages or salaries and may depend on lower transfer payments, widening the income gap between employed and unemployed households.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why can unequal ownership of assets lead to income inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: Assets prevent their owners from receiving any income.

options.label: B
options.text: Assets remove the trade-offs between alternative productive uses.

options.label: C
options.text: Households without assets necessarily earn greater wages than asset owners, because fewer assets guarantee higher labour earnings.

options.label: D
options.text: Assets generate income through rent, interest and dividends.

explanation: Wealth can generate income. If asset ownership is concentrated, the associated flows of property and financial income will also tend to be concentrated.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: How can inheritance contribute to wealth inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: Inheritance turns accumulated assets into current wage payments.

options.label: B
options.text: Inheritance distributes identical asset holdings to every household.

options.label: C
options.text: Inheritance transfers concentrated asset holdings across generations.

options.label: D
options.text: Inheritance reduces all wealth distributions to complete equality.

explanation: Inheritance can preserve or widen differences in asset ownership because some households receive substantial wealth while others receive little or none.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which factor is most likely to widen wage inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: A reduction in skill shortages

options.label: B
options.text: Improved access to vocational training that permits low-paid workers to obtain the skills demanded in higher-paid occupations

options.label: C
options.text: Poor access to vocational training for low-paid workers

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in employment opportunities for the unemployed

explanation: Limited training can keep productivity and employability low for some workers while skilled workers remain scarce and better paid, widening earnings differences.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which policy change is most likely to reduce inequality of disposable income?

options.label: A
options.text: Making the income tax system more progressive

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing transfer payments to low-income households

options.label: C
options.text: Reducing the minimum wage

options.label: D
options.text: Raising the threshold at which inheritance tax begins to apply

explanation: A more progressive income tax system takes a larger proportion of income from higher earners and tends to narrow differences in disposable income.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What is the main redistribution objective of a minimum wage?

options.label: A
options.text: To increase the market value of household assets.

options.label: B
options.text: To reduce the total money circulating in the economy.

options.label: C
options.text: To raise low-paid workers' earnings if they retain jobs.

options.label: D
options.text: To prevent inherited asset holdings being transferred across generations by reducing the amount of wealth left in estates.

explanation: A minimum wage sets a legal floor for wages. If it raises the pay of low-paid workers without large job losses, it can reduce income inequality.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What is a transfer payment?

options.label: A
options.text: A payment without a current factor service.

options.label: B
options.text: A payment for the use of land.

options.label: C
options.text: A payment a firm makes to a lender as remuneration for providing the funds used in production.

options.label: D
options.text: A payment for labour supplied to firms.

explanation: Transfer payments redistribute purchasing power rather than reward current production. Examples include unemployment benefits and some state pensions.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which statement describes a progressive income tax?

options.label: A
options.text: The proportion of income paid in tax falls as income rises.

options.label: B
options.text: Each person pays the same amount of money in income tax, regardless of how much annual income that person receives.

options.label: C
options.text: Only inherited assets are taxed.

options.label: D
options.text: The proportion of income paid in tax rises as income rises.

explanation: With progressive income taxation, higher-income earners pay a higher percentage of their income in tax, tending to narrow disposable-income differences.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which tax most directly targets wealth passed between generations?

options.label: A
options.text: A specific indirect tax

options.label: B
options.text: A sales tax

options.label: C
options.text: Income tax

options.label: D
options.text: Inheritance tax

explanation: Inheritance tax is imposed on wealth transferred at death above the rules or thresholds set by government, so it can reduce the intergenerational concentration of wealth.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What is a likely purpose of a capital tax in redistribution policy?

options.label: A
options.text: To guarantee automatic increases in every transfer payment.

options.label: B
options.text: To redistribute concentrated asset holdings or capital gains.

options.label: C
options.text: To replace progressive income taxes with proportional taxes.

options.label: D
options.text: To guarantee a statutory minimum hourly labour payment.

explanation: Capital taxes apply to capital or wealth-related assets or gains. They can reduce the after-tax accumulation of wealth among those holding larger asset stocks.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: How can state provision of essential health services reduce inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: Public finance removes the opportunity cost of health provision.

options.label: B
options.text: Public provision lowers the price barrier to essential treatment.

options.label: C
options.text: State financing automatically equalises the market value of every household’s assets without requiring any change in their ownership.

options.label: D
options.text: Public provision equalises the money income of every household.

explanation: State provision can redistribute in kind. Access to essential services no longer depends solely on ability to pay, and the benefit is often large relative to a low-income household’s income.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What is a possible disadvantage of setting a minimum wage above the market equilibrium wage?

options.label: A
options.text: Firms may reduce employment as labour becomes more costly.

options.label: B
options.text: Firms must reduce hourly wages for every existing employee.

options.label: C
options.text: Households must experience higher inequality in inherited asset values.

options.label: D
options.text: All workers withdraw their labour at every possible wage because a legal minimum prevents them from receiving any higher wage.

explanation: An effective minimum wage raises the cost of employing low-paid labour. If employers reduce the quantity of labour demanded, some workers may lose jobs, weakening the redistributive effect.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: How do transfer payments most directly reduce income inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: They increase the disposable income of eligible recipients.

options.label: B
options.text: They directly raise the market value of all household assets, including assets owned by recipients who receive no payment.

options.label: C
options.text: They convert income into capital.

options.label: D
options.text: They lower the legal minimum wage.

explanation: Cash transfers add to recipients’ disposable income. When targeted toward low-income households, they narrow the gap between lower and higher disposable incomes.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which feature makes an income tax system more progressive?

options.label: A
options.text: Identical tax percentages apply at every income level.

options.label: B
options.text: Income taxes are levied exclusively on purchases of goods.

options.label: C
options.text: Higher-income households pay larger percentages of their income.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower-income households pay larger percentages of their income.

explanation: Progressivity is about the proportion of income paid in tax. The average tax rate rises with income.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why may free state education reduce inequality over time as well as immediately?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower access costs improve current welfare and future earnings.

options.label: B
options.text: Free provision gives every household identical physical capital holdings.

options.label: C
options.text: Free provision removes the scarcity of resources used in teaching.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower access costs guarantee identical wages in every future occupation.

explanation: State education is an in-kind benefit that reduces current access barriers. By improving human capital, it may also increase future earning opportunities for people from lower-income households.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO2 Analysis

prompt:
A household receives wages of $36 000 a year, owns a house worth $240 000 and has savings of $20 000. Which statement is correct?
| Item | Amount |
| annual wages | $36 000 |
| house value | $240 000 |
| savings balance | $20 000 |

options.label: A
options.text: Wages are income; house and savings are wealth.

options.label: B
options.text: All three are income because they have money values.

options.label: C
options.text: Only savings are wealth; the house has no asset value.

options.label: D
options.text: House value is income; wages and savings are wealth.

explanation: Wages are measured over a year and are therefore an income flow. The house and savings are assets held at a point in time and form part of the household’s wealth.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A person owns shares worth $80 000. Their market value rises to $92 000, but no shares are sold and no dividend is paid. What has happened?

options.label: A
options.text: Wealth is unchanged and share income rises by $12 000.

options.label: B
options.text: Wealth and share income are unchanged at their original levels.

options.label: C
options.text: Wealth is unchanged and a transfer payment is received.

options.label: D
options.text: Wealth rises by $12 000 without share income being received.

explanation: The higher market value raises the stock value of the shares and therefore wealth. With no dividend or other receipt during the period, there is no current income flow from the shares.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A household saves part of its current income each year. What is the most direct link between income and wealth?

options.label: A
options.text: Saving reduces the value of accumulated household assets.

options.label: B
options.text: Saving converts accumulated assets into current wage income.

options.label: C
options.text: Saving makes household income identical to household wealth.

options.label: D
options.text: Saving adds to the stock of accumulated household wealth.

explanation: Income is a flow, but income that is not consumed can be saved and added to financial assets. In this way repeated saving can accumulate wealth over time.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An elderly person owns a valuable mortgage-free home but receives only a small pension. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The pension is part of wealth rather than income.

options.label: B
options.text: The house value is a flow of income each year.

options.label: C
options.text: The person must be both income-rich and wealth-rich.

options.label: D
options.text: The person may be wealth-rich but income-poor.

explanation: A valuable house creates a high stock of wealth, while a small pension implies a low current income flow. Income and wealth therefore need not rank people in the same way.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.1 difference between income as a flow concept and wealth as a stock concept | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Country A has an income Gini coefficient of 0.29 and a wealth Gini coefficient of 0.61. What does this show?

options.label: A
options.text: The country has a perfectly equal income distribution.

options.label: B
options.text: Average wealth must be twice the average annual income.

options.label: C
options.text: Wealth has greater measured inequality than the income distribution.

options.label: D
options.text: Income has greater measured inequality than the wealth distribution.

explanation: The higher Gini coefficient indicates the more unequal distribution. The coefficients do not compare the absolute amounts of wealth and income.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.2 measuring income and wealth inequality: Gini coefficient (calculation not required) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Country B has a Gini coefficient of 0.51 and country C has 0.34. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Average income must be higher in B.

options.label: B
options.text: Every person in C has the same income.

options.label: C
options.text: The measured distribution is more unequal in B than in C.

options.label: D
options.text: Country B must have more wealth in total.

explanation: A higher Gini coefficient indicates greater inequality. It does not establish the average or total amount of income or wealth.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.2 measuring income and wealth inequality: Gini coefficient (calculation not required) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country’s Gini coefficient falls while its average income also falls. What can be concluded?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower average income invalidates the observed Gini coefficient.

options.label: B
options.text: Relative inequality has fallen despite lower average income.

options.label: C
options.text: Every household necessarily experiences the same income reduction.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower average income necessarily raises relative income inequality.

explanation: The Gini coefficient concerns distribution, not average income. It is possible for an economy to become more equal while average income is falling.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.2 measuring income and wealth inequality: Gini coefficient (calculation not required) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Real income per head doubles in an economy but its Gini coefficient is unchanged. What is consistent with this information?

options.label: A
options.text: The distribution has necessarily become more unequal.

options.label: B
options.text: The Gini coefficient measures only the change in real income per head.

options.label: C
options.text: The relative degree of income inequality is unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: All income differences have disappeared.

explanation: An unchanged Gini coefficient means the measured relative inequality is unchanged. Average incomes can change substantially without the Gini coefficient changing.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.2 measuring income and wealth inequality: Gini coefficient (calculation not required) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Two countries both have a Gini coefficient of 0.40. Country X has much higher income per head than country Y. Which conclusion is valid?

options.label: A
options.text: Y necessarily has greater wealth than X.

options.label: B
options.text: X necessarily has lower inequality than Y.

options.label: C
options.text: Every household receives the same annual income in both countries because identical Gini coefficients guarantee identical individual incomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Measured inequality matches despite different average incomes.

explanation: Gini coefficients can be identical even when average income levels differ greatly. The measure captures relative distribution, not living standards by itself.

prompt: A new technology greatly increases the productivity of highly trained workers but has little effect on low-skilled workers. What is the most likely effect, other things equal?

options.label: A
options.text: Low-skilled workers necessarily receive higher income from dividends.

options.label: B
options.text: Differences in wealth necessarily disappear through technological progress.

options.label: C
options.text: Skilled labour demand rises and may widen wage differentials.

options.label: D
options.text: Differences in wages necessarily disappear through technological progress.

explanation: If technology raises the productivity and derived demand for skilled labour more than for low-skilled labour, skilled wages may rise relative to other wages, increasing income inequality.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why can regional differences in employment opportunities create income inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: Fewer local jobs automatically raise everyone's asset values.

options.label: B
options.text: Fewer local jobs can reduce employment and earnings.

options.label: C
options.text: Employment opportunities affect assets without affecting income flows.

options.label: D
options.text: Fewer local jobs automatically raise everyone's wage rates.

explanation: Where jobs are scarce, more people may be unemployed or accept lower-paid work. Regions with stronger labour demand can therefore have higher household incomes.

prompt: Two workers have the same hourly wage, but one works 40 hours per week and the other 15 hours. What can this contribute to?

options.label: A
options.text: Both workers earn the same total annual labour income because equal hourly wages eliminate the effect of different working hours.

options.label: B
options.text: Different earned incomes despite identical hourly wage rates.

options.label: C
options.text: Different definitions of wealth despite identical asset holdings.

options.label: D
options.text: Different individual Gini coefficients despite identical wage rates.

explanation: Income from employment depends on both the wage rate and the amount of work supplied. Differences in hours worked can therefore create income differences even at the same hourly wage.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why can successful entrepreneurship contribute to income inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: Different entrepreneurial outcomes produce different profit incomes.

options.label: B
options.text: Equal-profit rules require entrepreneurs to receive identical incomes.

options.label: C
options.text: Entrepreneurs' profits represent asset stocks rather than income flows.

options.text: Saving current income cannot add to wealth, because households acquire assets only through inheritance rather than their own earnings.

options.label: C
options.text: Saving transforms households' assets into government transfer payments.

options.label: D
options.text: Higher incomes can finance more saving and asset accumulation.

explanation: A household with a high income often has more scope to save after consumption. Repeated asset accumulation and returns on those assets can widen wealth differences over time.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country has equal wage rates for workers with the same skills, but a large gap in household income remains. Which factor could explain it?

options.label: A
options.text: A Gini coefficient showing complete equality between households.

options.label: B
options.text: Equal working hours combined with identical asset-income receipts.

options.label: C
options.text: Unequal work opportunities, working hours or asset-income receipts.

options.label: D
options.text: Measuring income as a flow received over time.

explanation: Household income includes more than hourly wages. Employment status, working time and property or financial income can create large differences even when comparable workers earn the same wage rate.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A government reduces vocational training while firms increasingly demand skilled labour. What is the most likely distributional effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower training narrows the wage gap between skill groups.

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing vocational training guarantees increased employment among low-skilled workers despite stronger employer demand for skilled labour.

options.label: C
options.text: Lower training equalises the asset holdings of all households.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower training can intensify skill shortages and wage differences.

explanation: Less training constrains the supply of skilled labour at the same time as demand is rising. Relative skilled wages can therefore increase, widening earnings differences.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An economy has rapid house-price growth and low home ownership among low-income households. Which effect is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Rising house prices affect income without affecting asset values.

options.label: B
options.text: Rising house prices necessarily equalise the entire income distribution.

options.label: C
options.text: Rising house prices give non-owners the same gains as owners.

options.label: D
options.text: Rising house prices benefit owners more than asset-poor non-owners.

explanation: A house-price rise is a wealth gain for owners. If ownership is concentrated among higher-income households, the gap in asset values can widen.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which mechanism best explains why inheritance can create a persistent cycle of inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: Recipients must consume every inherited asset immediately, preventing them from retaining investments or generating future income.

options.label: B
options.text: Inherited assets can support investment and future income generation.

options.label: C
options.text: Inherited assets prevent recipients from saving any future income.

options.label: D
options.text: Inherited assets eliminate differences in wealth between succeeding generations.

explanation: Inherited resources can provide both an initial asset advantage and access to opportunities that generate future earnings or returns, allowing inequality to persist across generations.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country cuts progressive income tax rates and transfer payments at the same time. What is the most likely effect on disposable-income inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: The two changes necessarily cancel exactly, leaving every household’s disposable income unchanged regardless of its previous tax and transfer position.

options.label: B
options.text: Both changes shift disposable income towards the poorest households.

options.label: C
options.text: Lower top taxes and lower bottom transfers can widen inequality.

options.label: D
options.text: Both changes affect household wealth without affecting disposable income.

explanation: Both changes move disposable income in the direction of greater inequality: lower progressive taxes raise after-tax income at the top, while lower transfers reduce income at the bottom.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why might an improvement in low-income households’ access to education reduce both income and wealth inequality over a long period?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher skills can improve earnings and subsequent asset accumulation.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher skills necessarily reduce the market prices of all assets.

options.label: C
options.text: Higher skills immediately transform income flows into fixed asset stocks.

options.label: D
options.text: Higher skills directly equalise inherited asset values across households.

explanation: Education can narrow earnings differences by improving productivity and job access. Higher lifetime income can also increase households’ ability to build wealth, affecting both distributions over time.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Average income rises by 10%, but almost all of the increase goes to the highest-income households. Which outcome is most plausible?

options.label: A
options.text: Income inequality rises even though average income increases.

options.label: B
options.text: Everyone’s income must have risen by 10%.

options.label: C
options.text: Income inequality must fall because average income rose.

options.label: D
options.text: The Gini coefficient must be unchanged.

explanation: An increase in the average says nothing about how the gain is distributed. If the increase is concentrated at the top, the relative distribution can become more unequal.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.3 economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country’s wealth is highly unequal mainly because a small group owns most productive assets. Which redistribution policy would most directly address this source of inequality?

options.label: A
options.text: A reduction in transfer payments to low-income households

options.label: B
options.text: A higher capital tax on concentrated asset wealth

options.label: C
options.text: A lower minimum wage

options.label: D
options.text: Higher user charges for state education

explanation: When inequality is driven by concentrated ownership of capital wealth, a capital tax directly reduces the after-tax value of that concentrated wealth. The other changes would reduce resources available to lower-income households rather than address the stated source.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A government raises the minimum wage substantially in a labour market with very elastic demand for low-skilled labour. Which assessment is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Wage regulation redistributes inherited assets rather than earned incomes.

options.label: B
options.text: Wage gains may be offset by low-paid workers losing jobs.

options.label: C
options.text: Wage regulation cannot affect firms' demand for low-skilled workers.

options.label: D
options.text: Wage gains guarantee more equal incomes irrespective of employment losses.

explanation: A higher wage floor has both a wage effect and a possible employment effect. When labour demand is very elastic, job losses may be large, so the lowest-income households can lose rather than gain.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: An economy has high unemployment among low-skilled workers. Which policy is more directly capable of raising the income of people who currently have no job?

options.label: A
options.text: Inheritance taxes rather than payments to unemployed households.

options.label: B
options.text: Minimum wage increases rather than payments to unemployed households.

options.label: C
options.text: Asset taxes rather than payments to unemployed households.

options.label: D
options.text: Transfer payments rather than higher minimum wage requirements.

explanation: A minimum wage directly benefits only workers who are employed at the wage floor. Transfer payments can reach people with no current wage income, making them more direct for unemployed households.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A country has moderate income inequality but extremely concentrated inherited wealth. Which tax change most directly addresses the stated problem?

options.label: A
options.text: A stronger inheritance tax

options.label: B
options.text: A lower inheritance tax and less progressive income tax

options.label: C
options.text: A lower minimum wage

options.label: D
options.text: A reduction in state education

explanation: Progressive income tax targets current income flows, while inheritance tax directly reduces the after-tax transfer of accumulated wealth between generations. The latter matches the source of the problem more closely.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A government wants to reduce both current income inequality and intergenerational wealth inequality. Which package is most comprehensive?

options.label: A
options.text: Minimum wages without any other redistribution policies.

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing the progressivity of income taxation and lowering taxes on inherited wealth while leaving transfers to low-income households unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: State provision of one service without other policies.

options.label: D
options.text: Progressive income taxes, transfers and taxes on wealth.

explanation: Income taxes and transfers affect current disposable income, while inheritance and capital taxes can act on accumulated or transferred wealth. A combined package therefore addresses both dimensions more directly.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: After a redistribution programme, the Gini coefficient falls but the real income of the poorest households also falls. What is the best judgement?

options.label: A
options.text: Changed average income makes the observed coefficient invalid.

options.label: B
options.text: Greater equality necessarily proves that absolute poverty fell.

options.label: C
options.text: Greater equality can coexist with falling bottom incomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Greater equality necessarily proves that poorest households became richer.

explanation: A lower Gini coefficient signals greater equality, not necessarily higher absolute incomes at the bottom. Policy evaluation therefore requires distributional and level information rather than the Gini coefficient alone.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A very high progressive income tax rate raises little additional revenue because high earners change behaviour and taxable income falls. What does this imply?

options.label: A
options.text: Behavioural changes necessarily reduce inequality to complete equality.

options.label: B
options.text: Behavioural changes may weaken the expected redistribution effect.

options.label: C
options.text: Higher statutory rates always guarantee more effective redistribution.

options.label: D
options.text: Higher income tax rates change the tax into inheritance taxation.

explanation: Redistribution depends on the tax actually collected and the behavioural response. If the tax base shrinks substantially, the government may collect less revenue and the intended reduction in disposable-income inequality can be weaker.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A government introduces inheritance and capital taxes, but wealthy households can legally reorganise assets to avoid much of the liability. What is the main implication?

options.label: A
options.text: Asset reorganisation automatically removes the effectiveness of minimum wages.

options.label: B
options.text: Asset reorganisation turns capital taxes into government transfer payments.

options.label: C
options.text: Avoidance can weaken the redistribution achieved by wealth taxes.

options.label: D
options.text: Asset reorganisation necessarily makes the wealth distribution more equal.

explanation: Taxes redistribute only to the extent that taxable wealth is actually reached. Extensive avoidance reduces revenue and the after-tax change in concentrated wealth holdings.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which circumstance most strengthens the case for state provision rather than cash transfers as the main redistribution policy for an essential service?

options.label: A
options.text: Access barriers remain that additional cash cannot adequately remove.

options.label: B
options.text: Government lacks productive resources to supply the essential service.

options.label: C
options.text: Only wealthy households make use of the essential service.

options.label: D
options.text: Affordable providers already serve every household without access barriers.

explanation: Cash transfers raise purchasing power, but they do not solve a shortage or geographic access problem. Direct state provision is more compelling when the service itself is unavailable to the target group.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A country has low wages at the bottom, concentrated inherited wealth and poor access to basic education. Which policy mix most closely matches all three problems?

options.label: A
options.text: Minimum wages, inheritance taxation and wider state education.

options.label: B
options.text: Income tax progressivity without asset taxes or education provision.

options.label: C
options.text: Cash transfers without wage regulation or education provision.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower minimum wages, lower inheritance taxation and higher education charges.

explanation: The wage floor targets low earned income, inheritance or capital taxes address concentrated wealth, and state education addresses unequal access to an essential service and future earning opportunities. No single policy in the alternatives covers all three sources.
reference: 3.3 Addressing income and wealth inequality | 3.3.4 policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage; transfer payments; progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes; state provision of essential goods and services | AO3 Evaluation
